intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for PowerPoint on Mac that you talk to. Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask about the slide in front of you, and Lazur answers out loud. It can circle a button, walk you through a feature one click at a time, and type text at your cursor. It is not a PowerPoint add-in, and it does not click for you.

Ask where a button is and Lazur circles it on your screen. You still do the click.
Ask how to do something and Lazur walks you through it one click at a time.

blocks.text: Most people who look for this want help with one slide at a time, not a new app to learn. The useful moments are small. You forget where a setting went. A chart reads badly. You need a line of speaker notes right now. Those moments are where a voice assistant earns its place.
What Lazur is and what it is not

Lazur is a voice assistant for macOS. It works in any app, PowerPoint included, because it looks at the screen you are using. It is not a plugin or add-in for PowerPoint, and it does not operate PowerPoint or any other app for you. The same shortcut works in other Mac apps, such as Keynote or Mail, because Lazur is not tied to one app. Windows is planned but not available, so this page covers Macs only.
What Lazur does on a PowerPoint slide

In PowerPoint, Lazur does three jobs. It explains what is on screen. It points at controls and walks you through features. It also drafts and dictates text. It cannot change the slide itself. You make every edit with your trackpad and keyboard, and Lazur tells you where to go.
Ask what is on the slide right now

Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask a plain question. Lazur answers out loud. Name the thing you can see, such as “What does this chart show?” or “Why does this title look cramped?” Keep the slide you mean in front of you when you hold the keys, because Lazur reads what is on screen at that moment.

Explanations help with the problems people report most. Decktopus ran a 2026 survey of more than 100 respondents, and SlideUplift reports that 58.1% named formatting as their top frustration when building slides. Another 52.3% named making data and charts look good. Treat these as a vendor-run survey reported secondhand, not as an official count.

Here is a worked example. You open a slide with a stacked bar chart. The legend sits on top of the bars, and you cannot tell which color is which. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask, “Why can’t I read this legend?” Expect an answer about the legend overlapping the plot area. Check that against your slide, because Lazur can misread a busy screen. Then you decide whether to move the legend or enlarge its font.
Find a button without digging through the ribbon

Ask, “Where is Morph?” and Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control on your screen. Morph is one of the topics Microsoft features in its PowerPoint help center, next to Presenter view and speaker notes. The circle saves a search through tabs. You still do the click yourself, which keeps you in charge of the file.
Walk through a feature one click at a time

Ask, “Walk me through the Morph transition,” and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on. That matters when a feature is buried in a menu, or when you use it once a quarter and forget the steps.

Keep PowerPoint in front while you follow along. The steps refer to what is on that screen, so a window that jumps to the front can confuse the guidance. If you get lost, ask “What do I click now?” and Lazur points at the next control.
Draft text at the cursor and dictate it

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur turns your speech into clean, formatted text and types it at the cursor, in any app. In PowerPoint, click inside a text box or the speaker notes pane first. Then hold fn, talk, and let go. The text lands where the cursor blinks, not where you were looking.

Lazur can also draft. Ask, “Draft three short speaker notes for this slide, plain and direct.” Lazur writes the text and types it at your cursor. Read every line before you present. Speaker notes are where errors hide, because nobody checks them until someone in the room asks about a claim.

Two features help with decks you build often. Snippets expand a short trigger into a longer block, such as a standard closing line. A personal dictionary teaches Lazur the product and client names it would otherwise get wrong. Clipboard slots hold text you reuse across slides.
Keyboard shortcuts worth learning first

Shortcuts are the fastest way to run a slideshow. Microsoft lists these on its support pages, and the presenting page says its shortcuts use the US keyboard layout. If you forget one, Lazur can explain it. It will not press it for you, so practice in a rehearsal instead of in front of a client.

blocks.text: Test each shortcut on your own Mac before a deadline. Layouts differ, and Microsoft's presenting list assumes a US keyboard. A shortcut that works on a colleague's machine may behave differently on yours.
Real problems people search for in PowerPoint on Mac

Microsoft does not publish a ranking of its most visited help topics, so no official data shows which problem people search for most. The PowerPoint help center features speaker notes, Presenter view, Zoom for PowerPoint, the Morph transition, and playing music during a slide show. Those topics match the jobs people bring to a presentation.

Survey data points the same way. In the 2026 Decktopus survey, as SlideUplift reports it, formatting leads, data and charts come second at 52.3%, and finding high-quality visuals follows at 47.7%. These are design problems. A spoken question is often quicker than hunting through menus.

items: Formatting: ask why text overflows a box or why the spacing looks off.
Charts: ask what a chart shows, or where the axis and legend settings live.
Presenting: ask how to start in Presenter View or blank the screen.
Speaker notes: draft or dictate notes straight into the notes pane.
Transitions: ask where Morph is and how to apply it to a slide.

blocks.text: When Lazur cannot help: crashes and damaged files

Lazur does not fix a PowerPoint that stops responding. Microsoft’s spinning wheel article is archived and refers to Office 2011, so read it as background only. It suggests checking the hard disk name. It also advises moving AutoRecovery files, since too many items can cause memory and save problems.

The same article suggests removing preferences, testing in a new user account, and testing in Safe Mode. Ask Lazur to explain any of those steps in plain language. Do not treat them as a guaranteed fix. Save a copy of the deck before you try any of them.
Check your Mac before you install

Office for Mac needs an Intel or Apple silicon Mac, 4 GB of RAM, 10 GB of free disk space, and a screen of at least 1280 x 800. Microsoft supports Office on the three most recent macOS versions. To keep receiving Microsoft 365 and Office updates, you need macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Older systems can still run Office, but they stop receiving updates, including security updates.

Version details matter on slides too. PowerPoint 16.107, released March 10, 2026, stopped saving a PNG fallback for each SVG in .pptx files. PowerPoint for Mac 16.13 and later support SVG directly. If a file size changed after that update, check this first.
How Lazur differs from Copilot in PowerPoint

Microsoft’s built-in AI for this job is Copilot in PowerPoint. Its release notes say it creates, edits and refines presentations from natural language, starting with version 16.109 on May 12, 2026. Microsoft 365 Copilot (Basic) provides it, and Premium adds brand kit templates and compliance checks. Check Microsoft’s pricing page for current costs.

The two do different jobs. Copilot builds and reworks the deck itself. Lazur explains what is on screen, points at controls, walks you through steps and dictates text at the cursor in any app. You can use both. Copilot can produce a first draft, and Lazur can help with the edits that follow.
What Lazur sees, and what leaves your Mac

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Memory of what you asked and did stays on your Mac.

Slides often hold client names, prices and unreleased plans. Check your company policy before you use any AI tool on a confidential deck. If the policy is unclear, ask the person who owns the deck before you open it in any assistant.
Mistakes people make in their first week

items: Letting go of the key too early. Lazur only looks while you hold the shortcut, so hold until the question ends.
Asking about a slide that is behind another window. Bring the slide to the front first.
Dictating with no text box selected. The text goes wherever the cursor is, so click the box first.
Expecting Lazur to click. It circles controls and guides you, but you do the clicking.
Skipping the Mac check. An older macOS stops receiving Office updates, so fix that before you use the tool on a client deck.

blocks.text: A first session, step by step

items: Download Lazur from the [download page](/download) and open it on your Mac.
Open a deck you know well, with at least one chart or a few text boxes.
Hold ⌥ ⌘, ask “What is on this slide?”, then let go and listen.
Ask “Where is the Morph transition?” and look for the circle.
Click inside a text box, hold fn, say one sentence, and let go.
Read the text back. Fix any mistakes before you move on.

blocks.text: Trial details are on the [pricing page](/pricing). For a rough check of how fast you talk compared with how fast you type, try the [speaking versus typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test). Then decide whether a voice assistant suits the way you build decks.

faq.question: Does Lazur work as an add-in inside PowerPoint?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that works across apps, PowerPoint included. It is not a plugin or add-in for PowerPoint or any other app, and it does not operate PowerPoint for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur click buttons in PowerPoint for me?
faq.answer: No. Ask where a control is and Lazur circles it. Ask how to do something and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You do the clicking and the editing.

faq.question: Which Mac and Office versions does this work with?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. For Office, Microsoft supports the three most recent macOS versions, and you need macOS 14 or later to keep receiving updates.

faq.question: Is Lazur free to try?
faq.answer: There is a free trial with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. Current plan prices are on the pricing page, so check there before you decide.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my slides all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Does it work with PowerPoint on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Windows is planned, but it is not available. This page covers Lazur on the Mac only.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix a PowerPoint that keeps crashing?
faq.answer: Not directly. Microsoft’s archived troubleshooting article suggests checking AutoRecovery files, testing in a new user account, and testing in Safe Mode. Save a copy of the deck before you try those steps.

faq.question: How is this different from Copilot in PowerPoint?
faq.answer: Copilot is Microsoft’s feature for creating and editing presentations from natural language. Lazur explains the screen, points at controls, walks you through steps and dictates text. Check Microsoft’s pricing page for Copilot costs.

faq.question: Will dictation work in speaker notes?
faq.answer: Yes, if the cursor is in the notes pane. Click inside the notes pane, hold fn, speak, and release. The text is typed at the cursor, the same way it works in any other app.
